title: SIADH with Severe Hyponatremia
sub: Small cell lung cancer · Medical oncology unit
profile: 72-year-old man with small cell lung cancer, admitted with nausea, headache and new confusion.

Notes: Admission 08:00

Client reports nausea, poor appetite, fatigue and a dull headache for 3 days. Wife says he has been "mixed up" since last night and is passing very little urine. Confused to time and place. Lungs clear. No edema. Mucous membranes moist.
Home medications
No diuretics. Completed first chemotherapy cycle 2 weeks ago.
Vitals: BP 158/92 mm Hg · HR 84 · RR 18 · SpO₂ 96% on room air · T 36.9 °C (98.4 °F)
81.6 kg today · 79.5 kg at oncology clinic 3 days ago
Urine 180 mL in the past 8 hours
Labs: Serum Na⁺ 118 mEq/L · Serum osmolality 252 mOsm/L · K⁺ 3.6 mEq/L · Glucose 104 mg/dL · BUN 9 mg/dL · Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
Urine osmolality 480 mOsm/L · Urine Na⁺ 52 mEq/L
Orders: Fluid restriction 800 mL/24 h · Strict intake and output · Daily weight · Neurological checks every 2 hours · Serum sodium every 4 hours · Notify provider for Na⁺ < 115 mEq/L or any change in neurological status

items.stem: Tap the findings in the record that match the key signs of water retention caused by excess antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
items.rationale: The book lists the key signs of SIADH as low urine output, hypertension, weight gain and confusion (from the low sodium). This client passed only 180 mL in 8 hours, gained about 2 kg in 3 days, has a BP of 158/92 and is newly confused. Clear lungs, normal temperature, a normal glucose and a recent chemotherapy cycle are not signs of ADH excess.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: The serum osmolality of 252 mOsm/L shows
opts: hemodilution from too much water in the blood
blanks.answer: hemodilution from too much water in the blood

blanks.pre: while the urine osmolality of 480 mOsm/L shows
opts: urine that is concentrated despite a low sodium
blanks.answer: urine that is concentrated despite a low sodium

blanks.pre: and the urine sodium of 52 mEq/L reflects
opts: high sodium loss in the urine
the kidneys holding on to sodium
blanks.answer: high sodium loss in the urine

items.rationale: In SIADH, too much water in the blood dilutes it, so blood osmolality falls below 275 mOsm/L (hemodilution). The kidneys keep reabsorbing water under ADH, so the urine stays concentrated even though the sodium is low, and sodium continues to be lost in the urine (urine sodium above 40 mEq/L). Dehydration would raise blood osmolality, and kidneys trying to save sodium would make urine sodium low, not high.

items.stem: Which complication is the client at highest risk for right now?
options: Seizures and coma from brain swelling as the sodium falls
items.rationale: The book states that neurological changes are the most critical concern in SIADH. Falling sodium lets water move into brain cells, and late symptoms are confusion, seizures and coma. This client is already confused with a sodium of 118 mEq/L. The client has too much water, not too little, so hypovolemic shock does not fit. The potassium is normal, and skin breakdown is a longer-term risk.

items.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.
rows: Count ice chips and IV fluids toward the 800 mL limit
Encourage 2 L of oral fluids to relieve his headache
Offer hard candy or gum for thirst and dry mouth
Aim to bring the sodium back to 135 mEq/L within 12 hours
items.rationale: The book's SIADH plan restricts fluid (600–800 mL/day), counts ice chips and IV fluid toward the limit, offers hard candy or gum for comfort, and starts seizure precautions when sodium is critically low. Encouraging fluids adds more free water and worsens the hyponatremia. Sodium must be corrected slowly, no more than 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours, to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome, so a rapid return to normal is unsafe.

items.stem: At 16:00 the sodium is 116 mEq/L and the client is drowsier. The provider prescribes 3% hypertonic saline. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Listen to lung sounds for crackles of pulmonary congestion
Increase the infusion rate if the next sodium has not risen
Keep the head of the bed flat or slightly elevated
Allow water as desired now that saline is infusing
Stop recording intake and output while the saline runs
items.rationale: Hypertonic saline is used when fluid restriction fails and must be given cautiously. The book says to monitor for pulmonary congestion and neurological symptoms, keep the head flat or slightly elevated, keep seizure precautions in place, and keep counting all fluids. Pushing the infusion faster risks correcting the sodium too quickly (more than 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours), which can cause osmotic demyelination. The fluid restriction still applies, so free water is not offered freely.

items.stem: The next morning the nurse reviews the client's progress. Which finding requires immediate follow-up with the provider?
options: Urine output 900 mL over the past 12 hours
Sodium risen from 116 to 131 mEq/L in 24 hours
Oriented to person, place and time
items.rationale: The goal is to correct the sodium slowly, no more than 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours, to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. A rise from 116 to 131 mEq/L (15 mEq/L) is too fast and must be reported now. A urine output that is picking up, a weight that is coming down and a client who is oriented again all show the treatment is working.

title: Addisonian (Adrenal) Crisis
sub: Gastroenteritis in known Addison disease · Emergency department
profile: 41-year-old woman with autoimmune Addison disease, brought in after 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea.

Notes: ED triage 14:10

Vomiting and watery diarrhea for 2 days; unable to keep her hydrocortisone tablets down since yesterday. Reports severe weakness, dizziness on standing and abdominal pain. Lethargic but answers questions. Skin dry with poor turgor. Darkened skin over the knuckles and elbows, which her husband says has been there for years. Says she has been craving salty foods.
History
Autoimmune Addison disease diagnosed 3 years ago. Home medication: oral hydrocortisone as prescribed.
Vitals: BP 76/44 mm Hg lying · HR 128 · RR 22 · SpO₂ 97% on room air · T 37.8 °C (100 °F)
Unable to stand for orthostatic readings: becomes faint on sitting up
Labs: Na⁺ 124 mEq/L · K⁺ 6.1 mEq/L · Glucose 48 mg/dL · BUN 41 mg/dL · Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL · Serum cortisol pending
Orders: Two large-bore IV lines · Hydrocortisone IV now (high dose, as prescribed) · 0.9% sodium chloride or D5NS bolus as prescribed, then reassess · Electrolytes and point-of-care glucose every 1–2 hours · Stool culture · Continuous cardiac monitoring

items.stem: Which findings require immediate follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
options: Darkened skin over the knuckles and elbows
items.rationale: The book lists the key features of an Addisonian crisis as severe hypotension, dehydration, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia and shock. A BP of 76/44, a glucose of 48, a potassium of 6.1 and a sodium of 124 all need action now. Darkened skin over the knuckles and salt craving are long-standing features of Addison disease, not signs of the acute crisis. A temperature of 37.8 °C is worth noting because infection can trigger crisis, but it is not the immediate threat.

items.stem: Which hormone deficit best explains the client's sodium of 124 mEq/L and potassium of 6.1 mEq/L?
options: Potassium loss from vomiting and diarrhea
items.rationale: The book links low aldosterone to hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and dehydration: without aldosterone the kidneys lose sodium and water and hold on to potassium. Low cortisol explains the fatigue, hypotension and hypoglycemia, not the electrolyte pattern. Excess ADH (SIADH) dilutes sodium but does not raise potassium. Vomiting and diarrhea lose potassium, so they would lower it, not raise it.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Give high-dose IV hydrocortisone as prescribed
Start rapid IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline or D5NS

items.rationale: A client with Addison disease who could not take her hydrocortisone, with severe hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia and hyponatremia, is in an Addisonian crisis triggered by fluid loss and illness. The book's priority interventions are high-dose IV hydrocortisone and rapid IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline or D5NS, while monitoring electrolytes and blood glucose. Myxedema coma causes hypothermia and bradycardia; thyroid storm causes high fever and hypertension. Fluid restriction would deepen the shock, and levothyroxine and cooling treat thyroid emergencies.

items.stem: For each intervention, indicate whether it is anticipated or not anticipated for this client.
rows: Rapid infusion of normal saline or D5NS
Fluid restriction to 800 mL per day
Point-of-care glucose and electrolytes every 1–2 hours
Stool culture to look for the cause of the diarrhea
items.rationale: The book's plan for Addisonian crisis is high-dose IV hydrocortisone, rapid IV fluids (normal saline or D5NS), close monitoring of electrolytes and blood glucose, and treating the underlying cause, here the gastroenteritis. Fluid restriction is the treatment for SIADH, and this client is dehydrated and in shock. Propranolol and cooling are thyroid storm treatments, and a beta-blocker would worsen her hypotension.

items.stem: IV access is established and the fluid bolus is running. Which prescription should the nurse carry out next?
options: Give her usual oral hydrocortisone dose with sips of water
Wait for the serum cortisol result before giving any steroid
Give a potassium binder before any other medication
items.rationale: The book's first priority intervention for Addisonian crisis is high-dose IV hydrocortisone, given along with rapid fluids. Oral tablets are not enough for a crisis, and this client cannot keep them down. Waiting for test results delays the hormone she is missing while she is in shock. A potassium binder does not replace the missing hormones; the potassium usually improves as fluids and hydrocortisone take effect, and it is tracked with the ordered electrolyte checks.

items.stem: Four hours later the nurse reassesses the client. Tap the findings that show the treatment is working.
items.rationale: The book says to monitor electrolytes and blood glucose in Addisonian crisis. A BP back to 104/66, a glucose of 96, a potassium of 4.8 and a sodium rising to 130 all show the hydrocortisone and fluids are reversing the crisis. Darkened skin is a chronic sign that will not change in hours. Continued loose stools mean the trigger still needs treatment, and a urine output of 15 mL/h is still low and needs follow-up.

title: Acute Kidney Injury with Hyperkalemia
sub: Nephrotoxic drugs and contrast dye · Medical unit
profile: 70-year-old man admitted 5 days ago with pneumonia, treated with IV gentamicin; had a contrast CT on day 2.

Notes: Client drowsy and intermittently confused overnight. Fine crackles at both lung bases. 2+ edema in both ankles. Says he is short of breath lying flat. Took ibuprofen at home most days for knee pain. Indwelling urinary catheter draining small amounts of dark yellow urine; bladder scan 40 mL. Pain 2/10 in the knees.
Medications
Gentamicin IV daily (day 5) · Ibuprofen 400 mg PRN (home medication continued on admission) · Contrast-enhanced CT chest on day 2
Vitals: BP 168/94 mm Hg · HR 92, occasional irregular beats · RR 24 · SpO₂ 93% on 2 L · T 36.8 °C (98.2 °F)
Urine 220 mL in the past 24 hours
Labs: K⁺ 6.4 mEq/L · BUN 68 mg/dL · Creatinine 3.6 mg/dL (1.0 on admission) · HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L · Na⁺ 133 mEq/L · Ca²⁺ 7.8 mg/dL
Muddy brown casts, renal tubular cells, protein 1+
Orders: Notify provider of K⁺ > 5.5 mEq/L · Sodium polystyrene sulfonate as prescribed · Sodium bicarbonate as prescribed · Strict intake and output · Daily weight · Fluid restriction as prescribed · Continuous cardiac monitoring · Nephrology consult for possible dialysis

items.stem: Tap the findings in the record that are red-flag symptoms of acute kidney injury.
passage: Fine crackles at both lung bases
items.rationale: The book's AKI red flags include oliguria (urine under 400 mL/day), sudden weight gain, crackles in the lungs, confusion or drowsiness from uremia, and peripheral edema. This client has all five. Knee pain of 2/10, a normal temperature and a small bladder scan volume are not red flags; the low bladder volume actually tells the nurse urine is not being held back by a blockage.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.
items.rationale: The book classifies AKI as prerenal (reduced blood flow), intrinsic (damage to kidney tissue) or postrenal (blocked urine flow). Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and contrast dye are listed as nephrotoxic causes of intrinsic AKI, and muddy brown casts point to tubular damage. The small bladder scan volume argues against a postrenal block, and nothing suggests blood loss or shock. With urine under 400 mL/day he is in the oliguric phase, the first of the three phases.

items.stem: Which complication poses the most immediate threat to this client's life?
options: Cardiac dysrhythmia from a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L
A new infection from the urinary catheter
Anemia from reduced red cell production
items.rationale: Hyperkalemia and cardiac dysrhythmias are both listed among the complications of AKI. A potassium of 6.4 mEq/L with irregular beats on the monitor can progress to a fatal dysrhythmia within minutes, so it comes first. Infection, anemia and progression to chronic kidney disease are real risks, but they develop over days to months.

items.stem: Which interventions should the nurse anticipate in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the provider to stop the gentamicin and ibuprofen
Give a 1 L IV fluid bolus to flush the kidneys
Track intake, output and daily weights
Teach a high-protein diet to support healing
Encourage bananas and orange juice for energy
items.rationale: The book's AKI management is to treat the cause and stop nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides), track intake, output and daily weights, watch for fluid overload in the oliguric phase, prevent and treat hyperkalemia, restrict potassium as needed, and use a high-carbohydrate, low-protein diet. A large IV fluid bolus would add to the fluid overload he already has. A high-protein diet adds to the waste his kidneys cannot clear. Potassium-rich foods would push the potassium higher.

items.stem: At 11:00 the nurse finds that no urine has drained into the catheter bag for 2 hours. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Request an extra dose of IV furosemide
Check the catheter and tubing for kinks or a blockage
Give a fluid challenge to test kidney response
Prepare the client for emergency dialysis
items.rationale: The book tells the nurse to check for catheter obstruction before assuming the AKI has worsened. A kinked or blocked catheter is a quick, reversible cause of zero output. Only after the catheter is confirmed to be working should the provider be told that output has stopped. Extra diuretic or a fluid bolus without knowing the cause could worsen the fluid overload or miss a simple fix.

items.stem: The next morning the nurse reviews the client's response to treatment. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or a need for further action.
rows: More difficult to rouse than yesterday
Crackles now heard to the middle of both lungs
items.rationale: The book gives sodium polystyrene sulfonate to lower serum potassium and sodium bicarbonate to correct metabolic acidosis, so a potassium of 5.0 and a bicarbonate of 21 show those treatments worked. A weight loss of 1.2 kg means fluid is coming off. Worsening drowsiness (rising metabolic waste) and crackles now heard higher in the lungs (pulmonary edema) are AKI red flags and need prompt follow-up, possibly for dialysis.

title: Increased Intracranial Pressure
sub: Traumatic brain injury · Neuro intensive care unit
profile: 34-year-old man admitted after a motorcycle crash with a traumatic brain injury; an ICP monitor was placed on admission.

Notes: Alert, oriented × 3, follows commands. GCS 15. Pupils 3 mm, equal and brisk. Reports mild headache. Sutured scalp laceration.

Difficult to rouse, opens eyes to voice, oriented to person only. GCS 12. Reports worsening headache. Vomited forcefully twice without nausea beforehand. Right pupil 5 mm and sluggish, left 3 mm and brisk. Found lying flat with head turned to the left and a pillow under his knees.
Vitals: BP 128/78 mm Hg · HR 82 · RR 16 regular · SpO₂ 98% on 2 L · T 37.1 °C · ICP 12 mm Hg
BP 142/80 mm Hg · HR 76 · RR 18 regular · SpO₂ 97% on 2 L · T 37.3 °C · ICP 24 mm Hg
Labs: Na⁺ 139 mEq/L · Glucose 118 mg/dL · Hgb 13.1 g/dL · Platelets 210,000/mm³
CT head on admission: right frontal contusion with surrounding swelling
Orders: Neurological checks and pupils every hour · Head of bed 30 degrees · ICP monitoring; notify for ICP > 20 mm Hg · Mannitol IV as prescribed for ICP > 20 mm Hg · Dexamethasone IV as prescribed · Stool softener daily · Suction as needed

items.stem: Which findings at 02:00 indicate that the client's intracranial pressure is rising? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: The book's early signs of increased ICP are a decreased level of consciousness, headache, pupil changes (sluggish, unequal) and nausea or vomiting that is often projectile. The ICP of 24 mm Hg is above the normal 5–15 mm Hg. The temperature, oxygen saturation and glucose are within acceptable limits and do not reflect pressure inside the skull.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: The first critical sign of worsening ICP is
opts: a drop in level of consciousness
blanks.answer: a drop in level of consciousness

blanks.pre: sign made up of a widened pulse pressure, irregular respirations and

items.rationale: The book stresses that a sudden drop in level of consciousness is the first critical sign of worsening ICP. Cushing's triad, a late sign, is a widened pulse pressure (rising systolic, falling diastolic), bradycardia and irregular respirations such as Cheyne-Stokes. Tachycardia is not part of the triad, and fixed, dilated pupils come late, not first.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Lay the client flat to improve blood flow to the brain
Elevate the head of the bed 30 degrees with the head midline
Suction for 30 seconds to clear the airway fully
Bend the hips with pillows under the knees for comfort

items.rationale: After a brain contusion, a falling level of consciousness, headache, projectile vomiting, a new unequal pupil and an ICP of 24 mm Hg point to increased intracranial pressure. The book's interventions include raising the head of the bed to 30 degrees with the head midline and neutral, and giving an osmotic diuretic such as mannitol as ordered. Level of consciousness is the first sign to change, and pupils go from sluggish and unequal to fixed and dilated as pressure rises, so both are tracked closely. Lying flat and flexing the hips raise ICP, and suctioning should be limited to 10–15 seconds. Meningitis and hypovolemic shock do not fit the history or vital signs.

items.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.
rows: Keep the head midline and neutral
Keep a pillow under the knees to flex the hips
Limit each suction pass to 10–15 seconds
Encourage him to bear down to move his bowels
Trend ICP readings and report values above 20 mm Hg
Keep the bed flat to lower blood pressure in the head
items.rationale: The book's ICP interventions are to keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees (not flat), keep the head midline and neutral, limit suctioning to 10–15 seconds, avoid hip flexion and straining, and monitor ICP when a device is in place. Turning the head to the side, flexing the hips with pillows under the knees and bearing down all raise intracranial pressure.

items.stem: The nurse is at the bedside at 02:00. Put the nurse's actions in order. Tap each in sequence; tap again to undo.
steps: Check the airway and oxygen saturation
Raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees, center the head and remove the knee pillow
Recheck level of consciousness, pupils and ICP
items.rationale: Airway and oxygenation come first on the book's list of ICP interventions, because low oxygen worsens brain swelling. Next, the nurse fixes the position he was found in: head of the bed to 30 degrees, head midline and the pillow removed from under his knees. This is quick and lowers ICP right away. Then the prescribed mannitol is given for the ICP above 20. Finally the nurse rechecks level of consciousness, pupils and ICP to see whether the steps worked.

items.stem: At 04:00 the nurse reassesses the client. Tap the findings that show the intracranial pressure is still rising.
passage: Urine output 350 mL in the past hour
items.rationale: The book's late signs of increased ICP are Cushing's triad (widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular Cheyne-Stokes respirations), fixed and dilated pupils, and posturing. A BP of 182/58 is a widened pulse pressure, and a heart rate of 50 is bradycardia. These need emergency action. The oxygen saturation and temperature are acceptable, and a large urine output is the expected effect of mannitol, not a sign of worsening.

title: Myasthenic Crisis
sub: Missed pyridostigmine doses during a viral illness · Emergency department
profile: 38-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis, brought in with increasing weakness and trouble breathing after a week of a cold.

Notes: ED triage 09:20

Has had a cold for a week. Missed her last two pyridostigmine doses because she could not swallow the tablets. Speaks in short phrases, with a weak, nasal voice. Drooping of both eyelids and double vision (her usual symptoms), now much worse. Cannot swallow her own saliva and is drooling. Weak cough. Breath sounds decreased at both bases. Masklike facial expression. Alert and oriented. Very anxious: "I can't get enough air."
Bowel
Last bowel movement yesterday, formed. No abdominal cramping.
Vitals: BP 136/84 mm Hg · HR 112 · RR 30, shallow · SpO₂ 86% on room air · T 37.6 °C (99.7 °F)
Unable to count past 8 in one breath
Labs: ABG: pH 7.31 · PaCO₂ 52 mm Hg · PaO₂ 58 mm Hg · HCO₃⁻ 25 mEq/L
WBC 11,200/mm³ · Na⁺ 138 mEq/L · K⁺ 4.0 mEq/L · Chest x-ray pending
Orders: Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92% · Continuous pulse oximetry · Respiratory therapy and anesthesia to bedside; prepare for intubation · Nothing by mouth · Pyridostigmine as prescribed (route per provider) · Neurology consult for plasmapheresis · Lorazepam IV as needed for anxiety · Morphine IV as needed for dyspnea

items.stem: Tap the findings in the record that require immediate follow-up by the nurse.
passage: Cannot swallow her own saliva and is drooling
Breath sounds decreased at both bases
items.rationale: The book identifies myasthenic crisis by hypoxia, notes decreased breath sounds from hypoventilation, and tells the nurse to prioritize maintaining the airway and preventing aspiration. An SpO₂ of 86%, decreased breath sounds, a weak cough and drooling because she cannot swallow her saliva all threaten her airway now. Drooping eyelids, double vision and a masklike face are typical, long-standing MG findings, and being alert and oriented is reassuring.

items.stem: Which explanation best fits the client's findings?
options: Cholinergic crisis from too much pyridostigmine
Myasthenic crisis from too little pyridostigmine
New Guillain-Barré syndrome after a viral infection
items.rationale: The book separates the two crises by cause: myasthenic crisis comes from undermedication and causes severe weakness, dyspnea and cyanosis, while cholinergic crisis comes from overmedication and causes weakness with diarrhea and bradycardia. She missed two doses, has a fast heart rate and no diarrhea, so this is myasthenic crisis. Her viral illness also worsens MG. Guillain-Barré syndrome does not explain a known MG history and missed doses, and anxiety does not cause hypoxemia with a high PaCO₂.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Support the airway and prepare for assisted ventilation
Give the anticholinesterase dose as prescribed by the provider
Give IV lorazepam to ease her breathing
Respiratory status: SpO₂, rate and effort
Ability to swallow and clear secretions

items.rationale: Missed doses with severe weakness, dyspnea and hypoxia point to myasthenic crisis. The book treats it by increasing the anticholinesterase (as prescribed) and puts airway management first in nursing care, with close monitoring of respiratory status and aspiration risk. Atropine and holding the medication treat cholinergic crisis, which would worsen this client. Sedatives such as lorazepam can worsen respiratory depression in MG. Blood glucose and daily weight do not track the threat to her breathing.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the admission orders. Which prescriptions should the nurse clarify with the provider before giving? Select all that apply.
options: Oxygen to keep SpO₂ at or above 92%
Lorazepam IV as needed for anxiety
Morphine IV as needed for dyspnea
items.rationale: The book warns to avoid sedatives, opioids and muscle relaxants in MG because they can worsen respiratory depression. Lorazepam (a sedative), morphine (an opioid) and cyclobenzaprine (a muscle relaxant) all need to be questioned for a client whose breathing is already failing. Oxygen, continuous pulse oximetry and nothing by mouth protect her oxygenation and her airway, and the pyridostigmine treats the undermedication behind the crisis.

items.stem: While waiting for the anesthesia team, the client begins to gurgle and cannot clear her secretions. Her SpO₂ is 84%. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give her pyridostigmine tablet with a sip of water
Sit her upright and suction her mouth and throat
Prepare her for a Tensilon (edrophonium) test
Give the prescribed lorazepam to slow her breathing
items.rationale: The book says to prioritize interventions that maintain the airway and prevent aspiration. Suctioning her mouth and throat with her sitting upright clears the airway right away. Giving oral tablets to a client who cannot swallow her saliva risks aspiration. A Tensilon test is a diagnostic step and does nothing for the blocked airway. A sedative would worsen respiratory depression.

items.stem: After intubation, plasmapheresis and an increase in her anticholinesterase dose, the nurse reassesses the client over 48 hours. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or needs follow-up.
rows: Stronger hand grip and a forceful cough
Three watery stools since the last dose
items.rationale: Stronger muscles, a better cough, good oxygenation and safe swallowing show the myasthenic crisis is resolving. New diarrhea and a heart rate of 52 are the book's signs of cholinergic crisis from overmedication, which can follow a dose increase. The book treats it by holding the anticholinesterase and giving atropine, so these findings must be reported right away.

title: Sickle Cell Vaso-Occlusive Crisis
sub: Dehydration after intense exercise · Emergency department
profile: 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease (HbSS), arriving with severe pain after a long soccer practice on a hot day.

Notes: ED triage 18:30

Severe aching pain in the lower back, both thighs and knees that began 4 hours after a 3-hour practice. Drank little water. Rates pain 9/10. Reports feeling very tired. Mucous membranes dry. No jaundice. Alert and oriented. Spleen not palpable. Says, "This is like my usual crises, just worse." Took ibuprofen at home without relief.
History
Sickle cell disease since infancy. Takes hydroxyurea daily. Last crisis 8 months ago. Baseline hemoglobin about 8 g/dL.
Vitals: BP 128/76 mm Hg · HR 118 · RR 22 · SpO₂ 92% on room air · T 38.3 °C (100.9 °F)
Labs: Hgb 7.6 g/dL · WBC 15,400/mm³ · Platelets 480,000/mm³ · Reticulocytes 9% · Urine specific gravity 1.030
Orders: Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 95% · IV 0.9% sodium chloride as prescribed · Morphine IV as prescribed for pain, reassess after each dose · Blood and urine cultures · Antibiotics as prescribed if infection suspected · Pain reassessment every hour

items.stem: Which findings require follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
options: Urine specific gravity 1.030 with dry mucous membranes
items.rationale: The book lists pain, fever and fatigue as the signs of a vaso-occlusive crisis and tachycardia on physical exam. Low oxygen and dehydration both trigger more sickling, so an SpO₂ of 92% and a urine specific gravity of 1.030 with dry mucous membranes need action. A hemoglobin of 7.6 is near his baseline and within the 5–10 g/dL range the book gives for sickle cell disease. His blood pressure and orientation are normal.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: This crisis was most likely triggered by

opts: sickle and block small blood vessels
swell and burst in the spleen
clump with platelets in large arteries
blanks.answer: sickle and block small blood vessels

items.rationale: The book names dehydration and intense exercise among the triggers that promote sickling. Sickle cell disease comes from inheriting two HbS genes; under low oxygen, red cells containing hemoglobin S become rigid and sickle-shaped and block small blood vessels, which causes the pain. Fetal hemoglobin protects against sickling, and that is why hydroxyurea is used.

items.stem: Which type of sickle cell crisis is the client most likely experiencing?
items.rationale: The book matches each crisis to its signs: vaso-occlusive (pain, fever, fatigue), sequestration (lethargy, pale skin, tachycardia), aplastic (fatigue, shortness of breath) and hyperhemolytic (jaundice, dark urine). Severe pain with fever and fatigue after dehydration fits a vaso-occlusive crisis. He has no jaundice, his hemoglobin is near baseline and his spleen is not enlarged, which argues against the other types.

items.stem: For each intervention, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.
rows: Give the prescribed IV analgesic within 30 minutes of arrival
Give aspirin for the fever and pain
Hold pain medication until the blood count results
Offer guided imagery and distraction along with medication
items.rationale: The book's treatment for a vaso-occlusive crisis is analgesia within 30 minutes, oxygen and hydration, with antibiotics when infection is suspected and non-drug pain strategies such as imagery and distraction alongside medication. Aspirin is to be avoided because of the risk of acidosis, and acidosis (low blood pH) itself increases sickling. Delaying pain medication until lab results return goes against the 30-minute goal.

items.stem: The IV line is in and the prescribed fluids are running. Put the nurse's next actions in order. Tap each in sequence; tap again to undo.
steps: Reassess the pain rating after the dose
items.rationale: Breathing comes first: his SpO₂ is 92% and low oxygen promotes more sickling, and applying oxygen takes seconds. The book then calls for analgesia within 30 minutes, so the prescribed IV morphine is given next. Pain is reassessed after the dose to judge whether it worked. Once the pain is easing, the nurse can coach imagery and distraction, which the book recommends alongside medication, not in place of it.

items.stem: Before discharge, the nurse reviews home care with the client. Which statements show the teaching was effective? Select all that apply.
options: "I'll drink fluids steadily all day, especially at practice."
"I can take aspirin at home if my joints start to hurt."
"Getting dehydrated, getting sick or being stressed can set off a crisis."
"I only need to push fluids once the pain starts."
"Hydroxyurea raises my fetal hemoglobin, which cuts down sickling and pain."
"I can stop hydroxyurea when I feel well."
items.rationale: The book's teaching is to keep a steady fluid intake, recognize triggers such as dehydration, infection and stress, and understand that hydroxyurea boosts fetal hemoglobin to reduce sickling and pain. Aspirin should be avoided because of the acidosis risk. Drinking only when pain starts misses the point of steady hydration, and stopping hydroxyurea between crises removes its preventive effect.
